notes.meaning: Matthew opens his book by setting down the family line of Jesus Christ, tracing him back to King David and Abraham. Calling Jesus the son of David presents him as the royal king promised to Israel, while calling him the son of Abraham points to God's promise to bless all nations through Abraham's family. This assures readers that God faithfully keeps the promises he made long ago.

The family line moves forward from Abraham to Isaac, then to Jacob, and then to Judah and his brothers. God chose Isaac rather than Ishmael, and Jacob rather than Esau, showing that his plan unfolds by his own choice rather than human customs. Judah is specifically highlighted because the promised king was foretold to come from his tribe.

Judah fathered Perez and Zerah by Tamar, and the family line continued through Perez down to Ram. Tamar was Judah's daughter-in-law, and her presence in the list recalls a painful and broken story from the Old Testament. God shows his deep grace by working through imperfect families and human failure to bring about the Savior.

The line passes from Ram to Amminadab, and from Amminadab to Nahshon and Salmon. Nahshon was a recognized leader of the tribe of Judah during Israel's journey through the wilderness after leaving Egypt. This shows how God preserved the royal family line during difficult generations in the wilderness.

Salmon fathered Boaz by Rahab, and Boaz fathered Obed by Ruth. Both Rahab of Jericho and Ruth of Moab were foreigners who turned to the true God in faith. Their place in the family tree shows that God's mercy extends beyond Israel to welcome outsiders into his family.

Jesse fathered David the king, and David fathered Solomon by the woman who had been Uriah's wife. David is singled out as the king because God made a special covenant promising an everlasting royal line through him. Mentioning Uriah's wife recalls David's great sin, reminding us that Christ entered a family line marked by human weakness and divine mercy.

The royal succession passed from Solomon through Rehoboam and Abijah down to Asa. Although the kingdom divided under Rehoboam because of sin and foolishness, God kept his promise to maintain David's line on the throne of Judah. Asa followed as a king who brought renewal by turning his heart toward God.

Asa fathered Jehoshaphat, who fathered Joram, and the line leads down to Uzziah. Matthew leaves out three wicked kings between Joram and Uzziah, which was a common practice in ancient Jewish family records. This reminds us that ancient genealogies often highlighted key ancestors rather than listing every single generation.

The royal line continued through Uzziah to Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. Even though Ahaz was an unfaithful king who led Judah into great trouble, his son Hezekiah became a godly reformer who trusted the Lord. God remained faithful to his covenant promise even when earthly kings proved unfaithful.

Hezekiah fathered Manasseh, who fathered Amon, who fathered Josiah. Manasseh was known for terrible evil before later humbling himself, while his grandson Josiah became one of Judah's most faithful and devoted rulers. God guided his chosen line through both dark and bright periods of Judah's history.

Josiah was the ancestor of Jeconiah and his brothers around the time when Judah was carried off into exile in Babylon. The term father here means grandfather, as Matthew passes over Jehoiakim. Even when the nation was conquered and the throne seemed lost forever, God did not let David's line disappear.

After the exile to Babylon began, Jeconiah fathered Shealtiel, who fathered Zerubbabel. Although the kings lost their crown and lived in captivity, Zerubbabel later became a leader who helped guide the people back to their homeland. God preserved the seed of David during the darkest days of foreign rule.

The family line moves through nine generations from Zerubbabel to Abiud, Eliakim, Azor, Zadok, Achim, Eliud, Eleazar, Matthan, and Jacob. These names do not appear in the Old Testament, but Matthew drew them from reliable public and family records. They reveal that God quietly guarded the line of the Messiah during centuries when no prophets spoke.

Jacob fathered Joseph, who is identified not as the biological father of Jesus, but as the husband of Mary. Jesus was born of Mary through a miracle, which made Joseph his legal and adoptive father according to Jewish law. This legal link gave Jesus full legal rights as the true heir to David's throne.

Matthew groups the entire history into three sets of fourteen generations, spanning Abraham to David, David to the exile, and the exile to the Christ. Dividing the ancestors into three equal groups served as a helpful memory aid for readers. The number fourteen also matches the value of the Hebrew letters in David's name, underlining that Jesus is the promised Davidic king.

Mary was pledged in marriage to Joseph, which in Jewish culture was a legally binding contract made before living together. Before their wedding was completed, she became pregnant by the power of the Holy Spirit. This miracle shows that Jesus came into the world with a real human nature, yet without inheriting human sin.

Joseph was a righteous man who sought to obey God's law, so he felt he could not complete the marriage under the appearance of unfaithfulness. However, because he was merciful and loved Mary, he chose not to bring her to public trial or shame her. He decided to give her a private divorce before just a few witnesses, combining a desire for righteousness with gentle mercy.

While Joseph wrestled with this painful decision, an angel appeared to him in a dream and called him the son of David. The angel told him not to fear taking Mary as his wife, because the child within her came from the Holy Spirit. God stepped in at the very moment of Joseph's deepest perplexity to give him clear direction.

The angel told Joseph that Mary would give birth to a son, and instructed him to name the child Jesus. The name Jesus means The Lord saves, which directly describes his great work. He did not come merely to deliver the nation from earthly enemies, but to save his people from the guilt and power of their sins.

Matthew points out that these events fulfilled the ancient prophecy delivered through the prophet Isaiah. Isaiah had announced that a virgin would conceive and give birth to a son whose name would be Immanuel, meaning God with us. Jesus fulfills this prophecy because he is God himself coming in human flesh to live with and rescue his people.

When Joseph woke up from sleep, he immediately obeyed the command of the angel and took Mary home as his wife. His prompt obedience proved that all his doubts and fears were put to rest by God's word. By taking her into his household, he bravely protected her honor and welcomed the child under his care.

Joseph kept Mary as a virgin until she gave birth to Jesus, ensuring that the miraculous nature of the birth could not be questioned. Once the child was born, Joseph named him Jesus, exactly as the angel had instructed him. Joseph showed steady and faithful obedience to God throughout the entire story.

differ.view: Many evangelicals believe the phrase until she gave birth implies that Joseph and Mary had a normal married life and other children after Jesus was born.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching holds that Mary remained a virgin throughout her entire life, and that the word until only describes the time leading up to the birth without implying marital relations followed.
